newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-GERMANY WIN QUARTER-FINAL PLACE.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-GERMANY WIN QUARTER-FINAL PLACE.

text.p: Germany emerged from the pack as a new challenger to Chinese supremacy in the women's team event at the world table tennis championships on Saturday.
The Germans went straight into the quarter-finals at the top of group C after defeating Taiwan 3-1 to complete a clean sweep of their five round-robin matches.

Germany, spearheaded by European champion Nicole Struse, laid the foundation of their success with hard-fought 3-2 victories over two of the strongest Asian teams -- Hong Kong, third in 1995, and North Korea who joined forces with the South in the joint Korean championship- winning team of 1991.
North Korea beat Hong Kong 3-0 in the battle for second place which took the Koreans through to the last 16 and Hong Kong through to the last 32.
China, who have won the event 10 of the last 11 times, predictably headed group A, maintaining a 100 percent record by beating Belgium 3-0 despite resting world champion Deng Yaping.

Japan, accused of cowardice by the Chinese for leaving out top player Chire Koyama in Friday's match against the champions, took no chances for the crucial clash with Russia which decided second place.
The Japanese won convincingly 3-0 and it was Koyama, world champion in 1987 as He Zhili of China, who got her adopted country off to a flying start.
South Korea had five wins to top group B ahead of Hungary, while Romania were also unbeaten in group D where Sweden finished second.
While the women's team event now enters the elimination stage, the men were scheduled to play two matches on Sunday before completing the group round-robins the following day.
Front-runners China and Sweden duly claimed their third victories in the early session but there were some hairy moments for the Swedes before they edged Belarus 3-2.

Vladimir Samsonov, who has climbed at breakneck speed to number four in the world rankings, really put the skids under Sweden who had won the title three times in succession before being dethroned by China two years ago.
Samsonov beat both Sweden's former world champions, destroying 1989 titleholder Jan-Ove Waldner 21-6 21-7 and 1991 holder Jorgen Persson 19-21 21-14 21-14.
European champion Waldner, the world number two, trailed 16-1 in the second game and could do nothing to break Samsonov's rhythm.
It was one of the heaviest defeats suffered by Waldner, who has the unique distinction of completing the men's grand slam of world championship, World Cup and Olympic gold.
Fortunately for the Swedes, Waldner recovered his composure to win the decisive match against Evgueni Chtchetinine.
The Chinese rested world champion Kong Linghui and Olympic champion Liu Guoliang but still strolled to a 3-0 success over Taiwan.
